planting.note: Direct sow in fall (or early spring in cooler climates) in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; unlike its relative miner's lettuce, Siberian miner's lettuce spreads by shallow rhizomes as well as self-seeding, forming a persistent shade groundcover rather than an annual colony.

directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian miner's lettuce is a Pacific Northwest and northern Asian native cool-season green, closely related to the round-leaved miner's lettuce but with pointed, spade-shaped leaves and dainty pink-veined white flowers held in loose sprays above the foliage from late winter into summer in cool, shaded gardens. The tender leaves and flowers have a mild, slightly tart, spinach-like flavor and are eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked, and the plant tolerates deeper shade than nearly any other salad green. Unlike annual miner's lettuce, it spreads by shallow rhizomes as well as self-seeding, gradually forming a low, semi-evergreen groundcover in a consistently moist, shaded woodland garden or the north side of a building. Thin or divide congested patches in fall to keep it in bounds, and expect it to die back in extended summer heat, returning with cooler fall weather.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in fall; bear's foot is a bold, large-leaved native of woodland edges and streambanks across the eastern and southeastern US and needs generous space for its coarse, sunflower-relative foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; bear's foot is a tall, coarse-textured native member of the aster family, its large, deeply lobed leaves giving the plant its common name and providing bold textural contrast in a woodland-edge or naturalistic border. From midsummer into fall it produces branched clusters of small, drooping, yellow, daisy-like flowers well above the foliage, attracting a range of native bees and other pollinators. It grows naturally along woodland edges, streambanks, and rich open slopes across the eastern and southeastern United States, tolerating both full sun and dappled shade as long as the soil stays reasonably moist and fertile. Give it plenty of room, since a mature clump can reach shoulder height or taller by late summer, and use it as a bold background plant behind smaller shade perennials rather than in a tidy front-of-border position.

subcategory: wild edible shoots / native climbing vine

planting.note: Plant root divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge, prairie margin, or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures; common carrionflower ranges farther into the central prairie states than the more Atlantic-coastal Smilax herbacea.

directions: Plant root divisions in rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland edge or shaded fence line where the tendril-climbing vine can scramble over shrubs or low structures. Common carrionflower is a thornless, herbaceous Smilax found from the Appalachians west across the prairie states and into the Rockies foothills, dying back to its tuberous rootstock each winter and resprouting reliably each spring, much like its more eastern relative Smilax herbacea. Young emerging shoots and tendril tips are harvested and cooked much like asparagus before the vine toughens, while the small, globe-shaped clusters of greenish flowers give off a mild carrion scent in late spring to draw in fly pollinators, followed by dark blue-black berries relished by birds. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established at a woodland or prairie-edge planting.
